blocks.text: Now, if one also wishes to hear the conjectures of others, in the Thesaurus of Pagninus alone ten interpretations of this word are to be found. "A bird," he says, "which some call the magpie, others the kite; Jerome, following the Greeks, the charadrius. R. Selomo says that it is דיה רגזנית, an irritable kite (rather, vulture). And it seems to me, he says, that it is what they call הירון heron, in Latin ardea. The Targum has אבו (ibbu), the kite, as some interpret it. You might also say the angry magpie. Some hold it to be the wood pigeon, others the woodpecker, others the jackdaw. Some of the more recent writers think it is the otus, of which Aristotle speaks in the History, book 8, chapter 12, which is so called from the little feathers standing out around its ears, as if eared. Some believe it is the hoopoe, because it comes closest to the charadrius, since it seems to bear a crest on its forehead." So says Pagninus, or Mercerus, who enlarged that Thesaurus considerably. And a third person could add much to both. For they had not seen the Syriac, which retains the Hebrew word, which Ferrarius's Syriac Lexicon explains as the porphyrio. Nor the Samaritan, in which anapha is ࠏࠎࠍࠉࠕࠀ, swallow. For Ajin stands there for Cheth, guttural for guttural, which is frequent in that translator. Nor the Arabic translators, of whom the two printed ones have here الببغا [al-babghā] albabga, or الببجة [al-babja] albabgia, the parrot, which the Greeks today call παπαγὰς [papagas], a word very like our own; and the two manuscripts العقاب [al-ʿuqāb] [III, 102] alokab, that is, eagle. Finally, of the three Chaldee versions they cite only one, namely Onkelos, by whom anapha is rendered אבו ibbu; but by the Jerusalem Targum it is rendered אבניתא abnitha (explaining the obscure by the more obscure), and by Jonathan דייתא אכמתא, black vulture. From this examination of the versions one may at least gather that the ancient translators had nothing certain about the true meaning of this word.

I will, however, say what seems to have moved Castellio, Junius and Tremellius, the French, English, Italians, etc., to interpret it with R. Selomo as heron. Aelian, History, book 5, chapter 36, to prove that the starry heron (asterias), tamed in Egypt, understands human speech to some extent, says: Εἴ τις αὐτὸν ὀνειδίζων δοῦλον εἴποι, ὅδε ὀργίζεται· καὶ εἴ τις ὄκνον καλέσειεν αὐτὸν, ὅδε βρενθύεται, καὶ ἀγανακτεῖ, ὡς καὶ εἰς ἀγεννὲς σκωπτόμενος, καὶ εἰς ἀργίαν εὐθυνόμενος [Ei tis auton oneidizōn doulon eipoi, hode orgizetai; kai ei tis oknon kaleseien auton, hode brenthyetai, kai aganaktei, hōs kai eis agennes skōptomenos, kai eis argian euthynomenos]; If someone abusively calls it a slave, it grows angry; and it is incensed and indignant at one who calls it lazy, as though low birth and sloth were being thrown at it in mockery. If there is any truth in this story, the heron was provoked not so much by the word as by the gesture of the one abusing it. However that may be, the vain and powerless anger of the heron is in no way to be compared with the anger of birds of prey, such as the eagle or the hawk, which, at the slightest provocation, at once swell with bile, blaze up, are all in a ferment, and strike with beak and talons. It is therefore certain that the name anapha, taken from anger, suits the heron far less than a bird of prey.

Let the same judgement be passed on those who translate it woodpecker, because Ovid writes in the Metamorphoses, book 14, fable 7, of Picus, king of Latium, recently changed by Circe's sorcery into the bird picus,
And, indignant that he had suddenly joined the Latin woods as a new bird, he strikes the wild oaks with his hard beak, and in anger wounds the long branches. [col. 340]

It is clear that the poet said this to serve his scene. For otherwise the Martius woodpecker, in Greek δρυοκολάπτης [dryokolaptēs], does not peck trees with its beak out of anger, but τῶν σκωλήκων, καὶ σκνιπῶν ἕνεκεν, ἵν᾽ ἐξίωσιν [tōn skōlēkōn, kai sknipōn heneken, hin᾽ exiōsin], for the sake of worms and gnats, so that they come out, as the Philosopher writes in the History, book 9, chapter 9. This, of course, is the food it lives on.

But why should the otus be called anapha, since it is not irascible, but κόβαλος [kobalos] and μιμητὴς [mimētēs], a buffoon and mimic, so that it is caught ἀντορχούμενος [antorchoumenos], dancing in turn opposite one who dances, as the Philosopher teaches in the History, book 8, chapter 12? But neither is there anyone for whom anapha is the otus, as Mercerus thought. Only the Jews of Germany render it in their language trapp, that is, the otis [bustard], not the otus:
